title: The Rise of Humanoid Robots in Everyday Life

slides.heading: The Rise of Humanoid Robots
slides.body: From sci-fi fantasy to factory floors — how humanoid robots are entering our daily world in 2026

slides.heading: What Makes a Robot 'Humanoid'?
slides.body: Humanoid robots have a human-like body plan — two arms, two legs, and a head. This design lets them use tools and spaces built for humans, from warehouses to home kitchens, without costly infrastructure changes.

slides.heading: From Labs to the Real World
slides.body: By 2026, Tesla's Optimus, Figure AI's Figure 02, and Boston Dynamics' Atlas have moved beyond demos. Thousands of units now work in auto plants, logistics hubs, and retail warehouses worldwide.

slides.heading: How They Learn to Move
slides.body: Modern humanoids learn through a mix of teleoperation and reinforcement learning. Human operators demonstrate tasks, and the robot's AI refines those movements through millions of simulated repetitions before touching the real world.

slides.heading: The Role of AI Brains
slides.body: Large vision-language models act as the robot's brain — interpreting scenes, understanding spoken instructions, and planning multi-step actions. The same AI revolution that powers chatbots now drives robotic hands and feet.

slides.heading: Jobs Gained and Jobs Shifted
slides.body: Humanoid robots are filling labor shortages in dangerous or repetitive roles — heavy lifting, night shifts, toxic environments. Economists note a shift rather than elimination: human roles move toward oversight, maintenance, and creative tasks.

slides.heading: The Cost Curve Is Falling Fast
slides.body: Early humanoid robots cost $200,000+. Scaled manufacturing and competition have pushed prices toward $30,000–$50,000, with projections of sub-$20,000 units by 2028 — comparable to a mid-range car.

slides.heading: Safety and Regulation Challenges
slides.body: Governments are scrambling to regulate robots that work alongside humans. Key issues include liability when a robot causes injury, data privacy from onboard cameras, and cybersecurity risks if a fleet is hacked.

slides.heading: Robots Coming Home?
slides.body: Consumer humanoid robots are the next frontier — handling chores, assisting the elderly, and acting as household helpers. Pilot programs in Japan and South Korea are already placing early models in care facilities and homes.

slides.heading: A Human-Robot Future
slides.body: Humanoid robots are no longer a distant promise. As the technology matures, the real work begins: designing a future where humans and robots collaborate safely, fairly, and productively.
